question: Why do you want to study Physical Education?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation connected to real experience with sport, movement, or teaching others, not just "I like sport."

bullets: Name a concrete experience that pulled you toward PE, not just a general love of sport
Show you understand PE is about more than playing well, it includes teaching, health, and development
Connect the motivation to what you want from the course itself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've played competitive badminton since I was ten, but what really pulled me toward this course was coaching a group of younger kids at my club last year and watching a shy girl who couldn't hit a serve become the most confident player in the group by the end of term. That's when I realised I care as much about how movement changes people as I do about performance itself. I want to study Physical Education because it sits right at that intersection of sport science and teaching, and I want to properly understand both sides.

commonMistakes: Saying only "I love sport" with no deeper reasoning
Talking exclusively about personal athletic achievement
Showing no awareness of the teaching or public-health side of PE
followUps: What part of that experience surprised you most?

question: Why do you want to study Physical Education at our university specifically?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course, not generic praise, plus a clear link to the applicant's own goals.

bullets: Reference something specific about the course structure, placements, or facilities
Connect that specific feature to a personal goal or experience
Show understanding of what distinguishes this course from similar ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What drew me here is the early school placement in first year rather than third, because I want to know quickly whether teaching is really the right path for me before I commit further. I also read about the biomechanics lab work built into the second-year modules, which fits how I like to learn, by testing an idea rather than just reading about it. Compared to other courses I looked at, this one treats teaching practice and sport science as genuinely equal rather than bolting a small teaching module onto a sports science degree.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any university's PE course
No mention of any specific module, placement, or feature
Focusing only on the city or campus rather than the course
followUps: What do you hope the early placement will show you about yourself?

question: Tell us about your own experience playing or coaching sport. What has it taught you?
lookingFor: A concrete account of hands-on involvement with sport, with genuine reflection rather than a list of achievements.

bullets: Describe a specific role, team, or coaching experience rather than a general summary
Reflect on a lesson learned, not just an outcome or trophy
Link the experience to why it makes you suited to studying PE
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've captained my school's hockey team for two years and this year I started assistant coaching an under-12s side on Saturday mornings. Coaching taught me something playing never did, that the same drill lands completely differently depending on how you explain it, and I had to learn to read the group rather than just repeat instructions louder. It's made me far more interested in the pedagogy side of sport, not just the performance side, which is a big part of why I want to study this properly.

commonMistakes: Just listing teams, positions, and trophies with no reflection
Describing coaching as easy or unremarkable
Not connecting the experience back to studying PE
followUps: What was the hardest part of coaching younger players?

subtopic: PE vs Sports Science vs Kinesiology
question: How would you describe the difference between Physical Education, Sports Science, and Kinesiology?
lookingFor: A reasonably accurate understanding of how the fields overlap and differ, showing the applicant researched the field, not just the course.

bullets: Describe PE as centred on teaching, pedagogy, and whole-population physical development
Describe Sports Science and Kinesiology as more focused on performance, biomechanics, and physiology research
Acknowledge the fields overlap heavily rather than drawing an artificial hard line
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As I understand it, Sports Science and Kinesiology are more focused on the science of movement and performance itself, things like biomechanics, physiology, and how to optimise an athlete. Physical Education shares that scientific base but adds the teaching and curriculum side, how you actually get a class of thirty different kids moving and learning, not just one athlete improving. In practice they overlap a lot, which is actually part of why I like PE, it doesn't force me to choose between the science and the people side.

commonMistakes: Treating the three fields as completely unrelated
Reducing PE to "just teaching games" with no science component
Being unable to say anything beyond the course title
followUps: Which of the three would you say you're personally more drawn to, and why?

question: Can you explain the FITT principle and how you'd use it to design a training programme?
lookingFor: Correct recall of Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type with a practical example of applying it.

bullets: Name all four components: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type
Explain briefly what each one adjusts in a programme
Give a simple practical example of manipulating one variable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type, and it's basically a checklist for adjusting a training programme so it keeps challenging the body. Frequency is how often you train, Intensity is how hard, Time is how long each session lasts, and Type is the kind of activity, like running versus resistance training. So if a beginner runner plateaus, rather than just telling them to run more, I'd think about which single variable to change first, maybe intensity through short intervals rather than just adding more mileage straight away.

commonMistakes: Getting one of the four letters wrong or forgetting one
Defining the terms but giving no practical example
Confusing FITT with a specific workout rather than a design framework
followUps: Which of the four variables would you change first for an injured athlete returning to fitness, and why?

question: What is progressive overload, and why does the body need it to improve?
lookingFor: Understanding that adaptation requires a gradually increasing demand, with awareness of the risk of overdoing it.

bullets: Define progressive overload as gradually increasing demand on the body over time
Explain why the body stops adapting once a stimulus becomes routine
Mention the balance needed between progression and injury or overtraining risk
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the demand you place on the body, whether that's more weight, more reps, more distance, or less rest, so that it keeps having a reason to adapt. The body is efficient, so once a certain load stops feeling challenging, it stops improving because it doesn't need to. The tricky part, which I find genuinely interesting, is that the increase has to be small enough to avoid injury or burnout but big enough to actually force adaptation, so it's as much an art as a science.

commonMistakes: Describing it simply as "doing more" with no mention of adaptation
Ignoring the injury or overtraining risk entirely
Confusing progressive overload with maximum effort every session
followUps: How would you explain progressive overload to a twelve-year-old in a PE class?

question: Name three major muscle groups used in running and briefly describe what each one does.
lookingFor: Reasonably accurate basic anatomical knowledge relevant to movement, not textbook-perfect precision.

bullets: Name at least three relevant muscle groups (for example quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, calves)
Give a simple, correct description of each muscle's role in the running motion
Show the answer comes from applied understanding, not just memorised terms
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The quadriceps at the front of the thigh extend the knee and drive the leg forward on each stride. The hamstrings at the back work opposite to that, bending the knee and helping pull the leg through during the swing phase. The glutes are probably the most underrated, they extend the hip and give a lot of the power behind each push-off, which is why runners with weak glutes often end up compensating with their lower back.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which muscle does flexion versus extension
Naming muscles with no description of their function
Only naming one muscle group instead of three
followUps: What might happen if one of those muscle groups was significantly weaker than the others?

question: What's the difference between cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance?
lookingFor: Clear distinction between whole-body aerobic capacity and a specific muscle's ability to sustain repeated contractions.

bullets: Define cardiovascular endurance as the heart and lungs' ability to supply oxygen over sustained effort
Define muscular endurance as a specific muscle group's ability to keep contracting without fatiguing
Give an example activity or test for each
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Cardiovascular endurance is about the heart and lungs, how well your body can keep delivering oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period, and it's usually tested with something like a beep test or a timed run. Muscular endurance is more localised, it's about how many times a specific muscle group can keep contracting before it fatigues, like how many push-ups you can do in a minute. You can have strong muscular endurance in your arms and still gas out on a long run because your cardiovascular system is the limiting factor there, not your muscles.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as interchangeable
Giving definitions with no example activity
Confusing endurance with maximal strength
followUps: Which of the two would matter more for a rock climber, and why?

question: Have you come across the term 'physical literacy'? What do you understand it to mean?
lookingFor: Evidence of wider reading beyond the school curriculum, and understanding that PE aims at lifelong competence and motivation, not just skill drills.

bullets: Define physical literacy as the motivation, confidence, competence, and knowledge to be active for life
Distinguish it from simply teaching sport-specific technical skills
Show why the concept matters for how PE should be taught
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Physical literacy is a term I came across doing wider reading before applying, and it basically means having the motivation, confidence, and competence to stay physically active throughout life, not just being good at a particular sport. It reframes PE's goal, instead of just producing kids who can hit a good tennis serve, the aim is that they actually enjoy movement enough to keep choosing it as adults. I find it a genuinely useful lens because it explains why a PE class that only serves the naturally athletic kids is actually failing at its real purpose.

commonMistakes: Confusing physical literacy with simply being fit or skilled
Being unable to explain the term beyond a vague guess
No link to why the concept matters for teaching practice
followUps: How would you design a lesson that specifically builds physical literacy rather than just sport skill?

question: Why do you think physical activity levels among young people have declined, and what role can PE play in addressing that?
lookingFor: Awareness of real contributing factors, with a realistic, non-preachy sense of what PE can and can't fix.

bullets: Identify plausible real contributors, for example screen time, reduced active travel, or school time pressures on PE itself
Position PE as one lever among several, not a total solution
Suggest a specific, realistic way PE could help
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of it comes down to how kids' free time has changed, more screen time, less active travel to school, and in a lot of schools PE time itself has actually been squeezed by academic pressure. I don't think PE alone can fix a problem that big, but I think it can shift a kid's relationship with movement if it's not just competitive team sport, which switches a lot of less athletic kids off entirely. Offering more variety, things like climbing or dance alongside football, seems like a realistic way PE could reach kids who currently opt out mentally the moment the whistle blows.

commonMistakes: Blaming young people for laziness with no structural context
Claiming PE alone can solve the problem
Vague statements with no concrete suggestion
followUps: Should PE be assessed and graded like other subjects? Why or why not?

question: How would you make a PE lesson inclusive for a class with a wide range of abilities, including a student with a physical disability?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of differentiation (STEP framework or similar) and a genuinely inclusive mindset, not a token gesture.

bullets: Mention adjusting space, task, equipment, or people (or an equivalent framework) rather than one-size-fits-all activities
Show the disabled student would be meaningfully included, not just given a passive role
Balance challenge for stronger students with accessibility for others
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd look at adjusting the task, the space, or the equipment rather than assuming one version of the activity has to fit everyone, so in a basketball lesson that might mean a lower hoop for some students or letting a student in a wheelchair play a wheelchair-basketball variant that everyone rotates through, rather than sidelining them to keep score. The key thing for me is that the adaptation has to be genuinely challenging for that student too, not just a way to keep them busy while everyone else does the real activity. I'd want every student leaving the lesson having actually been tested, just against an appropriate bar.

commonMistakes: Suggesting the disabled student simply sits out or scores
Offering only vague good intentions with no concrete method
Ignoring the need to still challenge the stronger students
followUps: How would you handle a student who resists an adapted version because they see it as 'easier' or embarrassing?

question: How would you try to motivate a student who consistently avoids taking part in PE lessons?
lookingFor: Empathy and a genuine attempt to understand the root cause before applying a strategy, not a blanket punishment or reward.

bullets: Start by trying to understand why the student is avoiding participation, rather than assuming laziness
Suggest a specific, low-pressure way to re-engage them
Show patience, recognising change may take time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to push harder, it would be to try to understand why, whether it's embarrassment about ability, body image, or just never having found an activity they enjoy. I'd try to find a low-pressure entry point, maybe giving them a role they feel more confident in first, like leading warm-ups or officiating, so they're still involved without the immediate pressure of performing in front of peers. I know that wouldn't fix it instantly, but building a small amount of trust and confidence first seems more likely to work than insisting they just join in.

commonMistakes: Assuming the student is simply lazy or unmotivated
Jumping straight to punishment or grade threats
Offering a generic answer with no specific first step
followUps: What would you do if that approach didn't work after a few weeks?

question: PE teachers often work closely with children in changing rooms and physical settings. What do you understand about safeguarding responsibilities in that context?
lookingFor: A mature, non-naive understanding that PE carries specific safeguarding responsibilities, without being alarmist or vague.

bullets: Show awareness that PE settings (changing rooms, physical contact, one-to-one coaching) carry particular safeguarding considerations
Mention the importance of clear boundaries, visibility, and following school policy rather than personal judgement alone
Avoid either dismissing the issue or being unrealistically dramatic about it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand PE puts teachers in situations that other subjects don't, changing rooms, physical contact when demonstrating or spotting, and time outdoors away from the rest of the school, so there's a real responsibility to keep things visible and follow clear boundaries rather than rely on gut feeling. I'd want to know a school's specific safeguarding policy properly rather than assume common sense is enough, because the point of a policy is that it protects both the student and the teacher. It's not something I find intimidating, it's just part of taking the role seriously.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the question as not relevant to them yet
Being vague with no concrete understanding of what safeguarding involves
Overdramatising the topic instead of giving a grounded answer
followUps: Why do you think safeguarding training is often more detailed for PE staff than for some other subjects?

question: Should school sport prioritise participation for everyone or competitive excellence for the strongest players? Where do you land on that?
lookingFor: A balanced, reasoned position that recognises the tension rather than picking an extreme without justification.

bullets: Acknowledge both participation and competitive development have real value
Explain a reasoned way to balance them, for example through different tiers of activity
Avoid a simplistic all-or-nothing answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think it has to be either-or, but I do think curriculum PE, the lessons every student takes, should prioritise participation and physical literacy, because that's the one place every child gets reached regardless of talent. Competitive excellence still matters and deserves real investment, but that's what extracurricular teams and squads are for, where students who want that intensity can opt in. The mistake I've seen schools make is letting competitive team selection bleed into ordinary lessons, so the less able kids end up standing on the wing the whole game, which defeats the point of compulsory PE.

commonMistakes: Picking one extreme with no acknowledgement of the trade-off
Giving a purely abstract answer with no practical distinction, like curriculum PE versus extracurricular teams
Dismissing competitive sport as unimportant
followUps: How would you handle a talented student who feels held back by a participation-focused lesson?

question: Have you read or watched anything recently related to sport, exercise science, or PE that made an impression on you?
lookingFor: Genuine evidence of curiosity beyond the school syllabus, with the ability to discuss it in some depth.

bullets: Name something specific, a book, article, documentary, or podcast, not a vague genre
Explain what idea or finding actually struck you
Show you can discuss it a little further, not just recite the title
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read an article about how PE lessons in some countries are being redesigned around long-term athlete development models instead of age-grouped competition, and it made me question something I'd never really thought about, that grouping kids purely by school year in sport can unfairly favour whoever happens to be born earlier in the academic year. It made me look into the research on relative age effect, which apparently shapes which kids even get selected for youth academies in the first place. It's stuck with me because it's such an invisible bias that has nothing to do with actual talent.

commonMistakes: Naming something vague like "sports documentaries in general"
Being unable to explain what actually interested them about it
Reciting a title with no genuine engagement or follow-up thought
followUps: Did that change how you think PE or youth sport should be structured?

question: Have you had any experience leading, officiating, or volunteering in a sports setting? What did you take from it?
lookingFor: Concrete evidence of hands-on involvement in organising or leading physical activity for others, with real reflection.

bullets: Describe a specific role, not a vague general claim of "helping out"
Mention a concrete challenge faced in that role
Reflect on what it taught them about leading others in a physical activity setting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been a sports leader at my school for the past year, running lunchtime activity sessions for younger year groups once a week. The biggest challenge was keeping thirty seven-year-olds engaged in one game without it dissolving into chaos, which taught me that clear, simple instructions matter far more than an elaborate plan. It's given me a much more realistic sense of what managing a group through movement actually involves, which is exactly the kind of thing I want to get properly trained in.

commonMistakes: Vague claims of volunteering with no specific detail
No reflection on what was learned
Overstating the scale of the role
followUps: What would you do differently if you led that session again?

question: Have you or someone you coached or played with ever dealt with a significant injury? How did you or they handle it?
lookingFor: Honest reflection on setback and recovery, showing maturity about the physical and mental sides of injury.

bullets: Describe a genuine injury situation with specific detail
Address both the physical recovery and the mental or emotional side
Show what was learned that applies more broadly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I tore ligaments in my ankle two years ago and was out of sport for four months, which was harder mentally than physically, I went from training five times a week to nothing overnight and felt genuinely low about it for a while. What helped was staying involved differently, I started helping the coach run drills from the sideline instead of disappearing from the sport entirely, which kept me connected and honestly gave me a completely new appreciation for the coaching side. It's part of why I'm now just as interested in supporting other people's development as I am in my own performance.

commonMistakes: Downplaying the emotional impact entirely
Describing the injury with no account of the recovery process
No broader lesson drawn from the experience
followUps: How did that experience change how you think about injury prevention?

question: What role do carbohydrates, protein, and fat each play in supporting physical activity?
lookingFor: Correct basic understanding of each macronutrient's primary role in exercise and recovery.

bullets: Identify carbohydrates as the body's primary and fastest-access energy source, especially for higher-intensity effort
Identify protein's role in muscle repair and growth after exercise
Identify fat as a longer-term energy store, particularly important for lower-intensity, longer-duration activity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are the body's go-to energy source, especially for anything higher intensity, because they're the fastest to convert into usable fuel. Protein's main role is repair and rebuilding, which is why it matters most after exercise, when muscle fibres have been broken down and need to recover stronger. Fat is more of a slow-burning, longer-term energy store, and it becomes relatively more important the longer and lower-intensity the activity is, like an ultra-marathon compared to a sprint.

commonMistakes: Saying fat is simply "bad" and has no useful role in performance
Mixing up which macronutrient supports immediate versus long-duration energy
Describing protein's role with no mention of repair or recovery
followUps: Why might a marathon runner and a sprinter have quite different dietary priorities?

question: Why do we warm up before exercise and cool down afterwards? What's actually happening physiologically?
lookingFor: Basic but accurate physiological reasoning, not just "to prevent injury" with no explanation of mechanism.

bullets: Explain the warm-up raises muscle temperature and heart rate gradually, improving elasticity and blood flow
Explain the cool-down helps gradually lower heart rate and assists circulation of blood back from the extremities
Connect both to reduced injury risk and better performance, not just tradition
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A warm-up gradually raises muscle temperature and heart rate, which makes muscles more elastic and improves blood flow to the areas about to be worked, so they're less likely to strain under sudden load. A cool-down does something similar in reverse, it helps bring the heart rate down gradually rather than stopping dead, which helps blood keep circulating back from the legs instead of pooling, and can reduce that light-headed feeling some people get after stopping suddenly. Both are really about managing the transition into and out of intense effort rather than shocking the system.

commonMistakes: Saying only "to prevent injury" with no physiological reasoning
Describing warm-up and cool-down as interchangeable
Treating it as pure tradition with no functional explanation
followUps: How might you adapt a warm-up differently for a strength session versus a distance run?

question: What's the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and why does that distinction matter in PE?
lookingFor: Accurate definitions with a real understanding of why intrinsic motivation tends to sustain lifelong activity better than external rewards.

bullets: Define intrinsic motivation as doing an activity for its own enjoyment or satisfaction
Define extrinsic motivation as doing it for an external reward, grade, or pressure
Explain why relying too heavily on extrinsic motivators in PE can backfire long-term
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Intrinsic motivation is doing something because you genuinely enjoy it or find it satisfying in itself, while extrinsic motivation is doing it for an outside reward, like a grade, a medal, or to avoid getting in trouble. It matters in PE because if a student only ever takes part to avoid punishment or chase a grade, that motivation tends to disappear the moment the external pressure is removed, which is probably part of why so many people stop exercising once they leave school. I think the real skill in teaching PE well is designing lessons that build some genuine enjoyment, not just compliance.

commonMistakes: Reversing the definitions of intrinsic and extrinsic
Treating extrinsic motivation as always bad with no nuance
Not connecting the theory back to a practical PE implication
followUps: Can extrinsic motivation ever help build intrinsic motivation over time? How?

question: A young athlete you coach asks you about using a supplement that's legal but sits in a grey area ethically. How would you respond?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that takes the athlete's question seriously while being clear about responsibility and long-term wellbeing.

bullets: Take the question seriously rather than dismissing or lecturing immediately
Distinguish between legality and what's genuinely appropriate for a young or developing athlete
Land on a clear, responsible position while explaining the reasoning, not just issuing a rule
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to actually understand why they're asking, whether it's pressure to perform, something they've seen older athletes use, or genuine curiosity, because the reason shapes the right response. I'd be honest that legal doesn't automatically mean appropriate, especially for a still-developing young athlete, and I'd want to talk through what's actually driving the desire for an edge rather than just saying no outright. My responsibility as a coach is their long-term development and health, not a short-term result, so I'd lean toward caution and involve a parent or a qualified nutritionist rather than giving a personal verdict myself.

commonMistakes: Giving a flat yes or no with no reasoning
Ignoring the athlete's underlying motivation for asking
Failing to acknowledge the coach's duty of care to a young athlete
followUps: Does your answer change if the athlete were an adult elite athlete instead of a young developing one?

question: What's your view on the growing use of wearable technology and data tracking in school and youth sport?
lookingFor: A balanced, thoughtful view weighing genuine benefits against risks like over-reliance on data or pressure on young people.

bullets: Acknowledge a genuine benefit, such as better-informed training or injury prevention
Raise a real concern, such as data anxiety, overtraining pressure, or reducing intuition
Reach a reasoned overall position rather than being purely for or against
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it has real value, heart rate and load data can genuinely help catch overtraining before it becomes an injury, which is hard to judge by feel alone. But I'm a bit wary of it in a school context specifically, because turning every session into a stream of numbers can create pressure or anxiety in young people who are still working out their relationship with their own body, and it risks them chasing the number instead of learning to actually read how they feel. I'd want it used as one input a coach considers, not something handed directly to a fourteen-year-old to obsess over.

commonMistakes: Being uncritically enthusiastic with no downside considered
Dismissing technology entirely as unnecessary
Giving a generic answer with no reference to the school or youth context specifically
followUps: How would you introduce this kind of technology responsibly in a PE class?

question: Physical Education can lead to teaching, coaching, sports development, or allied health routes like physiotherapy. Where do you currently see yourself heading, and why?
lookingFor: A grounded, honestly reasoned direction with awareness that the course can open multiple paths, not an over-rehearsed single answer.

bullets: Give a genuine current direction with a reason behind it
Show awareness that the degree opens several realistic paths, not just one
Demonstrate openness to the direction evolving as they learn more
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I lean toward secondary school teaching, because coaching those younger players last year made me realise I get more satisfaction from someone else's improvement than my own. But I know that could shift, the placement modules might show me I prefer working one-to-one with athletes, which would point more toward coaching or sports development instead. I like that this course doesn't force that decision immediately, it lets me test the different routes with real experience before I commit.

commonMistakes: Naming only one narrow path with no awareness of alternatives the course offers
Sounding rehearsed or over-certain about a ten-year plan
No reasoning behind the stated preference
followUps: What would make you change your mind about that direction?

question: A completely sedentary adult asks you to help them start exercising for general health. What would you consider when designing their first few weeks?
lookingFor: Applied reasoning that shows understanding of graded progression, injury risk, and adherence, not just handing over an advanced programme.

bullets: Start with low intensity and frequency, prioritising consistency and injury avoidance over rapid gains
Consider the person's current health, any medical concerns, and realistic time availability
Build in a genuine progression plan and something that keeps them motivated to continue
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd resist the temptation to give them an ambitious plan straight away, because the biggest risk for a sedentary adult isn't underworking, it's injury or burnout that makes them quit in week two. I'd start with something like two or three short sessions a week of low-impact activity, walking or light cycling, and check for any medical concerns or doctor clearance first if there's any doubt. From there I'd build gradually using something like the FITT principle, and I'd make sure at least part of it is something they actually enjoy, because a technically perfect plan is useless if they stop doing it after a month.

commonMistakes: Designing an intense programme unsuitable for a true beginner
Ignoring medical history or health screening entirely
No consideration of long-term adherence or enjoyment
followUps: How would you know if the plan needed adjusting after the first few weeks?

question: If you were redesigning your old school's PE curriculum from scratch, what would you change, and why?
lookingFor: Original, well-reasoned thinking about curriculum design that goes beyond simply criticising, showing genuine engagement with what PE is for.

bullets: Identify a specific, genuine shortcoming from real experience, not a generic complaint
Propose a concrete alternative rather than just criticism
Reason about the trade-offs of the proposed change
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My school ran almost entirely on traditional team sports, football, rugby, netball, which meant if you weren't naturally built for those, PE became something to survive rather than enjoy. I'd introduce a rotating block of less common activities, things like climbing, dance, or badminton, specifically because they reward different physical strengths and give more students a chance to genuinely feel good at something. The trade-off is it needs more staff training and equipment than just rolling out a ball, but I think it's worth it if the actual goal is getting more students to keep being active after they leave school, not just fielding a good school team.

commonMistakes: Only criticising with no concrete proposed alternative
A generic answer disconnected from real experience
Ignoring practical trade-offs like cost, staffing, or facilities
followUps: How would you convince a sceptical head teacher that this change was worth the cost and disruption?
